title: Tragedy of the commons

definition.text: The idea that when people share a resource that benefits each user at a cost to everyone, each person has a reason to overuse it, so together they use it up.

facts.text: English economist William Forster Lloyd described the problem in an 1833 pamphlet about herders sharing a common pasture, where adding extra cattle could lead to overgrazing.
The name comes from a 1968 essay in the journal Science by ecologist Garrett Hardin, who took his title from Lloyd's pamphlet.
Hardin's main worry was human overpopulation, and he wrote that 'freedom in a commons brings ruin to all'.
The commons problem is used as a model for many resource problems today, including water, forests, fish, and oil, gas and coal.
Climate change has been described as a huge example of the tragedy, with the Earth treated as a commons whose resources are depleted without regard to the harm done to others.
Proposed government fixes include privatization, regulation such as permits for fishing or logging, and making users pay for the harm they cause.

Elinor Ostrom and colleagues found the tragedy less common and easier to solve than Hardin claimed, because local users often design their own rules; a Swiss Alpine commons has been run by farmers since 1517.
Critics note that historical English common land always had a legal owner, and only people with legal rights, called commoners, could use it.

contested_note: Scholars dispute whether overuse is inevitable: Ostrom's work is seen by some economists as refuting Hardin, and others say open, unregulated common land never really existed.
distinct_from: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

title: Commons dilemma

definition.text: A kind of social dilemma in which people's short-term selfish interests clash with the long-term interests of the group and the common good.

facts.text: Researchers study, in the laboratory and the field, when groups under- or over-harvest common resources.
When people harvest in a fixed order, those who go first take more than those who follow.
People take less from a common pool when others can see them than when they act anonymously.
Selective punishments for overuse, such as installing water and electricity meters in houses, can encourage conservation.

distinct_from: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

title: Comedy of the commons
article: Tragedy of the commons#Comedy of the commons

definition.text: The case where a shared resource becomes more valuable to each user the more people use it, so 'the more the merrier'.

facts.text: Legal scholar Carol M. Rose described the idea in a 1986 article, giving commerce and group recreation as examples.
Rose argued that such 'comedic' public resources are more likely to suffer from too little investment than from overuse.

distinct_from: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

title: Solutions to the tragedy of the commons

definition.text: The range of ways, from local self-organized rules to government action, proposed for stopping people from overusing a shared resource.

facts.text: Finding solutions to the tragedy of the commons is counted among the main problems of political philosophy.
Turning a common resource into private property gives the new owner a reason to keep it productive, an idea linked to Coase in 1960.
Privatization works when the owner pays the full price of using up the resource.
Governments can cap how much of a shared resource any one person may use, for example through permits for mining, fishing, hunting, grazing and logging.
Government solutions are used when a community is too large for its social ties to hold it together.
A middle way shares ownership between government and community, so that no one or two parties hold all the power.
Political scientist Robert Axelrod argues that even self-interested people often find ways to cooperate, because restraint serves both them and the group.

title: Common-pool resource

definition.text: A natural or human-made resource system, such as fishing grounds or an irrigation system, that is costly but not impossible to keep people from using.

facts.text: Unlike pure public goods, common-pool resources get crowded or overused because what one user takes is no longer there for others.
Examples include forests, irrigation systems, fishing grounds, groundwater basins, pastures and the atmosphere.
Without management, each fisher has a reason to catch as many fish as possible before someone else does, so fish stocks soon run down.
They may be owned by governments as public goods, by communities as common property, or by individuals and firms as private goods; when no one owns them they are open access.
Elinor Ostrom found many such resources run by local self-managing communities, contradicting the claim that they must be privatized or be destroyed.
In James Bay, Quebec, beaver numbers recovered after Indigenous communities' customary hunting laws were legally recognized and outside trappers were banned.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Resource stock and flow

definition.text: The split of a shared resource into a core stock that must be protected and a flow of units, such as fish or grass, that can be harvested from it.

facts.text: As long as the stock is not harmed, it keeps regrowing the flow, so careful use can continue indefinitely.
Taking more than the flow shrinks the stock, which in turn shrinks future flows; sometimes the loss cannot be undone.
A pasture can be grazed a certain amount each year without harm, but overgrazing makes it prone to erosion and less useful.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Common property regime

definition.text: A social arrangement by which a community regulates how a shared resource is kept up, maintained and used.

facts.text: It is not the same thing as a common-pool resource, since such resources are not always governed as common property.
Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the total benefit of the resource, and they protect the core resource while sharing out what can be harvested.
Community members have monitored access, while outsiders can be kept out, so the resource looks private to outsiders and common to insiders.
Rules must limit the amount, timing and technology of harvesting: limits set too high destroy the resource, and limits set too low waste benefits.
It differs from open access: in a common property system access is not free, so the resource looks private to outsiders and common to insiders.
Such systems arise when users acting alone threaten the resource's total benefit, and usually work locally to prevent overexploitation.
Hardin's tragedy of the commons was criticized for not distinguishing common property from open-access resources.
Members' local knowledge often lets these regimes outperform rules designed by outside experts, and results are best when they also consult governments and experts.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons
notes: Article could also be 'Common-pool resource#Common property protocols'; facts draw on both sections.; Phrase concept with no page of its own.

title: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

definition.text: Eight conditions that Elinor Ostrom found in long-lasting community arrangements for managing shared resources.

facts.text: The first principles are clearly defined boundaries, and rules for taking and supplying the resource that fit local conditions.
Most users should take part in making the rules, and monitors should be users themselves or answer to them.
Rule-breakers face sanctions that grow step by step, and conflicts can be settled cheaply and easily.
Authorities such as the government must at least recognize the users' right to organize, and large resources are run as layers of nested groups with small local ones at the base.
Ostrom set out this work in Governing the Commons (1990), showing that communities around the world have managed shared resources successfully through local governance.

title: Adaptive governance of common-pool resources

definition.text: A way of managing shared resources that Ostrom recommended for problems that are complex, uncertain and fragmented.

facts.text: Because management depends on the type of resource, a strategy that works in one place may not suit another.
Ostrom's five requirements are good timely information, ways to handle conflict, users who help monitor rule-keeping, flexible infrastructure, and readiness to adapt and fix errors.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Open access resource

definition.text: A resource that no one owns and that anyone can use, where what one person takes leaves less for others.

facts.text: Open access goods need little oversight or are hard to restrict, and because they are first come, first served, they are prone to the tragedy of the commons.
In an open fishery, profits draw in more fishers, leaving fewer fish; scarcer fish raise prices, which draws in still more fishers.
Hardin's work has been criticized for failing to tell common-pool resources apart from open access resources.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Four types of goods

definition.text: A grid that sorts goods by two questions, whether people can be kept from using them and whether one person's use leaves less for others.

facts.text: Goods that can be withheld and are used up, such as food, clothing and parking spaces, are private goods.
Goods that cannot be withheld but are used up, such as fish stocks and timber, are common-pool resources.
Goods that can be withheld but are not used up, such as cinemas, software and private parks, are club goods.
Goods that cannot be withheld and are not used up, such as free-to-air television, air and national defense, are public goods.

distinct_from: Ostrom's design principles for the commons

title: Free-rider problem

definition.text: A market failure that happens when people who benefit from a shared resource or public good pay nothing, or too little, for it.

facts.text: A coastal town's lighthouse helps ships from many countries, even though those ships pay nothing toward its costs.
Because no one can be kept from using a public good, each person has little reason to help pay for it.
Free riding leads to too little of a good being produced or too much being used up, which is wasteful for society.
When asked how much money they would pay for a public good, people tend to understate how much they value it.
Even though people tend to cooperate by nature, the presence of free riders has been shown to make cooperation break down.
Climate change is often framed as a free-rider problem: every country gains from others cutting emissions, but each would lose by switching to a low-carbon economy itself.
Shown as a prisoner's dilemma, if two people should share the cost of a fire station and both refuse to pay, society gets nothing.
Low-cost pooling of contributions, as in internet crowdfunding where no money changes hands until a goal is met, is one way around the problem.

distinct_from: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism
notes: S:09bccf850fc4 carries a DISPUTED - DISCUSS tag; not used.

title: Assurance contract

definition.text: An agreement in which people pledge money toward a public good only if enough others also pledge; otherwise the good is not built and the money is returned.

facts.text: In a dominant assurance contract, an entrepreneur refunds pledges plus an extra sum if the target is missed, and earns a fee if it is met.
This makes pledging the best move for each person whatever others do, which game theory calls a dominant strategy.
First proposed by Bagnoli and Lipman in 1989, they work best in small groups of easily identified people, and crowdfunding sites such as Kickstarter use them.

distinct_from: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism

title: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism
article: Free-rider problem#Introducing an exclusion mechanism (club goods)

definition.text: Using laws such as copyright and patents to stop people copying an information good, turning a public good into a club good.

facts.text: These laws can solve free riding, but they give owners monopoly power, so the result is not fully efficient.
In the United States, patent rights encourage drug companies to charge prices above the cost of making one more dose.

title: Social sanctions against free riders
article: Free-rider problem#Non-altruistic social sanctions (common property regimes)

definition.text: Punishments that group members impose on those who use a shared resource without contributing, as a way to keep cooperation going without the state.

facts.text: Punishing costs the punisher, so groups often reward members who sanction free riders.
Paying for enforcement is not perfectly efficient, but it is often cheaper than letting the resource run down.
People sometimes punish free riders even without any reward, though whether such costly punishment explains cooperation is disputed.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether costly punishment of free riders can explain cooperation.
distinct_from: Intellectual property as an exclusion mechanism

title: Property rights

definition.text: The rules that decide who owns a resource or good and how it may be used.

facts.text: Resources can be owned by individuals, associations, collectives or governments.
Property rights have three parts: the right to use a good, the right to earn income from it, and the right to sell, change, abandon or destroy it.
Well-enforced property rights give people reasons to invest, innovate and trade, which makes markets work better.
Governments can create property rights through direct rules such as discharge limits, or through market tools such as taxes and tradable permits.
An emissions trading scheme works by setting up property rights for the atmosphere.
Secure rights make resources harder to exploit, so people are less likely to use them unsustainably.
Studying former European colonies, Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson found strong evidence that institutions giving secure property rights lead to prosperity.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm

title: Types of property regimes

definition.text: The main ways a resource can be held, open access, public, private or common property, sorted by whether others can be kept out and whether use leaves less for others.

facts.text: Open-access property is owned by nobody, nobody manages it and access is not controlled; an unregulated forest is an example.
Open access can exist because ownership was never set up in law, or because keeping people out costs more than it is worth.
Public or state property is owned by the public, with access and use controlled by a government agency.
Private property is controlled by its owner or owners; a cellphone is an example because only one person can use it and it must be bought.
Common or collective property in the legal sense is owned by a group whose members jointly control access, use and exclusion.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm
notes: Section is internally inconsistent: S:54d163ef76af calls public property excludable, while its example S:d6601afe0802 (a pavement) is called non-excludable; S:08a4186c998e equates open access with 'common property resource'.

title: Lockean labor theory of property

definition.text: John Locke's idea that a person who mixes their labor with an unowned resource comes to own the result, as long as enough of as good quality is left for others.

facts.text: Locke set out the theory in his Second Treatise of Government (1689), starting from the claim that each person owns their own self.
The condition that 'enough and as good' must remain for others is called the Lockean proviso.
Libertarians cite the tragedy of the commons as what happens when governments forbid people to claim resources in the Lockean way.

distinct_from: Property rights theory of the firm

definition.text: A good is rival when one person's use of it stops or reduces others' use of it at the same time.

facts.text: An apple is rival: once one person eats it, no one else can.
A good is non-rival when serving one more person costs nothing extra; a TV broadcast, a scenic view, clean air and street lights are examples.
Non-rivalry does not mean a good is cheap to provide in total, only that the cost of one more user is zero.
Roads, the internet and courts are non-rival only up to a point, after which congestion slows everyone, so economists now treat rivalry as a scale rather than a yes-or-no.
Paul Samuelson introduced non-rival consumption in 1954 to tell private from public goods, and Richard Musgrave later added rivalry and excludability as criteria.

definition.text: A good that becomes more valuable to each user the more other people use it.

facts.text: Steven Weber introduced the idea in 2004, noting that free and open-source software gets better for everyone as more people use it.
Any natural language is anti-rival, because it is more useful the more people speak it.
Efforts against climate change are perversely anti-rival: a free-riding country still gains from others' efforts.

definition.text: A good that people can be kept from using, usually by charging them, but that one person's use does not reduce for others until it gets crowded.

facts.text: Examples include cinemas, cable television, software as a service, and gym, golf club or swimming pool memberships.
Serving one more user costs almost nothing, so club goods are often supplied by natural monopolies and are kept artificially scarce.
Providers exclude non-payers either to cover fixed costs, as nonprofits do, or to make a profit.
Controlling access nearly always causes a deadweight loss, such as the cost of tollbooths or digital rights management.
The European Union has been treated as a club good: its services can be withheld from non-members, while adding members to the Schengen Area does not make travel harder for existing ones.

definition.text: The branch of economics, founded by James M. Buchanan in 1965, that studies how big a group sharing a good should be and how it should share the costs.

facts.text: Buchanan saw a gap between purely private and purely public goods: excludable goods shared by more people than a private good but fewer than a public one.
Each new member lowers the cost per head but adds congestion, so there is an optimal club size that gives members the most benefit.
Cornes and Sandler's conditions lead to two-part pricing: a fixed membership fee plus a charge per use.
Olson and Zeckhauser (1967) applied the theory to cost-sharing in NATO, asking whether some members were free riding.

title: Coase theorem

definition.text: The claim that when one party's activity harms or helps another, the two can bargain their way to an efficient outcome, whoever starts with the property rights, provided bargaining costs are low enough.

facts.text: If true, the theorem would let private individuals solve externality problems by themselves.
Coase developed it while thinking about radio stations interfering with each other: the station that gained more from broadcasting would pay the other not to interfere.
If fencing the farm is cheaper than fencing the cattle, bargaining should produce a fence around the farm whether the farmer or the rancher holds the rights.
In his 1960 paper Coase himself argued that real transaction costs are rarely low enough for efficient bargaining.
Imperfect information and poorly defined property rights can also block the bargain.
In Danish talks between waterworks and farmers, farmers used their information advantage to seek over-compensation and drag out talks, showing how sensitive the theorem is to transaction costs.
Behavioral economist Richard Thaler found that people care about fairness when bargaining over their own property, so they may reject efficient but unfair deals.

contested_note: Critics argue the theorem rarely applies in practice, and Duncan Kennedy argues that the starting allocation of rights always matters.
distinct_from: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

title: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

definition.text: The two separate claims inside the Coase theorem: that bargaining gives an efficient result, and that it gives the same result whoever starts with the rights.

facts.text: Coase did not set out a single formal theorem; others built the loose formulation from his work.
Later authors showed the invariance claim is not generally true, because who bears liability changes wealth, which in turn changes demand and prices.
Steven Cheung extended it in 1969: without transaction costs, contracts, markets and corrective taxes can all reach the same efficient result.

title: Coasean bargaining failures
article: Coase theorem#Criticisms of the applicability of the theorem

definition.text: The practical reasons why private bargaining over harms such as pollution often fails to reach the efficient outcome the Coase theorem predicts.

facts.text: The assignment problem: with a polluted river it is hard to tell which factories caused the harm and who was hurt, and victims tend to overstate their losses.
The holdout problem: when many people hold rights, the last one can demand more, so everyone has a reason to demand more and bargaining unravels.
When many parties benefit equally from a deal, each has a reason to free ride by withholding payment.
In twenty legal nuisance cases studied by Ward Farnsworth, no party tried Coasean bargaining, out of anger at the unfairness of having to bargain.

distinct_from: Efficiency and invariance versions of the Coase theorem

definition.text: How far the supplier of a good can stop people who have not paid from using it.

facts.text: Economists describe every good by two traits: how excludable it is and how rival it is.
A cinema film is excludable: ushers check tickets, so non-payers cannot see it.
A lighthouse is non-excludable, because any ship at sea can use its light.
Paul Samuelson proposed the idea in 1954 as a yes-or-no trait; Elinor Ostrom in 1990 recast it as a scale from fully excludable to fully non-excludable.
Music, films and software are semi-excludable: they have a price, but piracy lets many non-payers use them.
Because producers cannot profit from goods people get free, non-excludable goods tend to be under-supplied without government help.

title: Public good

definition.text: A good or service that no one can be kept from using and that one person's use does not reduce for others, usually supplied by government and paid for by taxes.

facts.text: Examples include knowledge, official statistics, national security, flood control systems, aids to navigation and street lighting.
Clean air and other environmental goods are common examples of public goods.
Because people who do not pay can still use them, public goods may be under-produced, overused or degraded: the free-rider problem.
Without government provision, such goods might be produced only in small amounts or not at all, since they are not profitable enough for private firms.
Paul Samuelson set out the modern theory in his 1954 paper The Pure Theory of Public Expenditure, building on Wicksell and Lindahl.
It is a misconception that public goods must come from the public sector: they can occur naturally or be produced by individuals, firms or community groups.
Pure public goods are rare, and economists debate how to define public goods and how serious the problems they cause are.
Technology can change a good's status: encryption lets broadcasters sell access, and cheaper road pricing allows charging by actual use.

contested_note: Economists debate whether 'public goods' form a real category at all, and how to define and measure public goods problems.

definition.text: Goods such as streets, libraries and education that share some traits of public goods but from which people can be excluded, and are therefore often misclassified.

facts.text: The lighthouse is the textbook public good, but Ronald Coase argued its costs could be profitably bundled into port fees, which has funded real lighthouses.
A community soccer field is a mixed case: the field is shared, but players bring their own gear and pay a rental fee.
Some goods, such as orphan drugs, need government incentives to be made yet are not public goods.

definition.text: Public goods whose benefits fall mainly on the people nearby, such as a clean office or a neighborhood crime watch, rather than equally on everyone.

facts.text: Overlapping neighborhoods are often modeled as a network; when neighborhoods do not overlap, the standard model is the Tiebout model.
A 2019 theory of public goods in networks found voluntary provision usually falls short of the efficient level, with a few people contributing heavily and their neighbors free riding.

title: Digital public goods

definition.text: Open-source software, data sets, AI models, standards and content that anyone can use, treated as public goods.

facts.text: The UN Secretary-General's Roadmap for Digital Cooperation defines them as open resources that follow privacy laws, do no harm and help reach the Sustainable Development Goals.
A small group of maintainers often keeps such projects going while many more users benefit, raising worries about burnout and underfunding.

notes: Peripheral to a nature-economy course; kept as Minor.

definition.text: One of the best-studied procedures for deciding how much of a public good to fund and who pays, based on what each person reports it is worth to them.

facts.text: Most work uses the Clarke pivot rule, which makes sure everyone pays in and no one is worse off for taking part.
It needs a great deal of information from each user, which, among other problems, has kept it from being used in practice.
Mechanisms like it were developed to draw out people's true valuations, since people have reasons to understate how much they value public goods.
Each participant is paid the total value of everyone else, so its own welfare matches society's and telling the truth is its best strategy.

title: Quadratic funding

definition.text: A recent way to fund public goods, developed by Buterin, Hitzig and Weyl from quadratic voting, in which each contributor gives a single amount and a subsidy tops up the total.

facts.text: Like the VCG mechanism it needs a subsidy, and there is always a deficit the designer must cover.
It is vulnerable to collusion between contributors and to fake identities (sybil attacks).

notes: S:b6c253ed1ef9 says the total is 'the sum of the square roots of individual contributions'; the standard formula is the square of that sum. Not used; verification pass should check.

definition.text: Funding a public good by selling lottery tickets, with all ticket money going to the good and the prize paid from outside funds.

facts.text: Lotteries are approximately efficient, and funding approaches the optimal level as the prize grows.
In very large populations, contributions through a lottery shrink toward those of plain voluntary giving and should fall to zero.

definition.text: The Weisbrod model's idea that nonprofit organizations supply public goods that government leaves unprovided.

facts.text: Government supplies what the median voter wants, which is less than citizens with stronger demand would like.
Nonprofits funded by donations from those citizens fill the gap.

definition.text: A cost of making a trade in a market, over and above the price of the thing traded.

facts.text: They fall into three groups: search and information costs, bargaining and decision costs, and policing and enforcement costs.
Douglass North argued that a society's rules, its institutions, largely set transaction costs, and institutions that keep them low can boost economic growth.
The term is often wrongly credited to Ronald Coase, though his 1937 paper The Nature of the Firm discussed the 'costs of using the price mechanism'.
John R. Commons introduced the idea in 1931 that transactions are the basis of economic thinking.
High transaction costs, such as proving additionality, have been a known difficulty of carbon offset schemes like the Clean Development Mechanism.

definition.text: Oliver Williamson's approach that studies the transaction itself and treats firms as structures for governing deals rather than just production machines.

facts.text: Unlike standard microeconomics, it assumes people have bounded rationality and treats property rights and contracts as problematic rather than costless to enforce.
Williamson named frequency, asset specificity, uncertainty, limited rationality and opportunism as what drives transaction costs.
Specialized investments cannot be redeployed if a contract ends, so ending such a deal causes significant loss.
Williamson was awarded the 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics.

definition.text: A kind of negotiation in which a buyer and a seller argue over the price or terms of a deal.

facts.text: If the two sides agree on terms, the trade goes ahead.
Bargaining has largely disappeared where fixed-price shops dominate, but remains common for expensive goods such as homes, cars and jewellery.
Emotions, mental biases and a sense of fairness strongly affect bargaining; the endowment effect makes sellers ask more than buyers will pay.
Coase argued that without transaction costs, people would bargain their way to the same use of resources however a court ruled in a property dispute.

definition.text: John Nash's answer to how two parties should split the gains from agreeing: the deal that maximizes the product of what each gains over failing to agree.

facts.text: Nash (1950) defined a bargaining problem as the set of possible agreements plus a disagreement point, what each gets if talks fail.
Bargaining solutions are usually built from axioms such as efficiency, symmetry and independence of irrelevant alternatives.
The Nash solution handles only the simplest structure and does not show how efficient outcomes are reached over time.
It picks the agreement that maximizes the product of each player's gain over the disagreement point, called the Nash product.

definition.text: A way of picturing property ownership as a set of separate rights, like sticks in a bundle, that can be split among different people and put back together.

facts.text: The idea began with Wesley Newcomb Hohfeld in 1913, though he never used the phrase.
The five traditional rights are possession, control, exclusion, enjoyment (use, including resource extraction) and disposition (transfer).
Parts of a right can be held separately: a tenant may live on land while someone else owns the minerals or water beneath it.
Governments keep rights such as environmental regulation, zoning and eminent domain, and third parties may hold rights such as conservation easements.

title: Common good (economics)

definition.text: In economics, a good that is rival (one person's use leaves less for others) but non-excludable (people cannot be kept from using it).

facts.text: Because anyone can use them, common goods risk being overexploited when people act in their own interest.
A road is a public good when empty, but once congested each extra driver slows others, turning it into a common good.
Fish stocks in international waters, among the least regulated common resources, are likely to be depleted if fish are taken without limits.
Aristotle already observed that 'what is common to many is taken least care of'.

notes: The page calls common goods a synonym of common-pool resources, while 'Common-pool resource' and S:f8082e4ff72b reserve that term for institutionally managed commons; ordering pass may fold this into 'Common-pool resource'. Section 'Common goods and normal goods' (S:33a65d90d75b, S:37c13835fbbf) is confused and was not used.

definition.text: A usually unpriced good from nature or green infrastructure, such as clean air and water, landscapes, parks, rivers, forests and beaches.

facts.text: Environmental goods are a sub-category of public goods.
They are hard to protect because users pay nothing up front and pollution can damage them indefinitely.
There is no agreed method for putting an economic value on them; obstacles include free riding, unclear ownership and the fact that they cannot be divided up.
Economists try to value them by asking people's willingness to pay, sometimes with simulated markets and contingent valuation, but critics cite framing effects and biases.
Alternative measures of progress, such as the Genuine Progress Indicator and Gross National Happiness, count environmental damage and resource depletion.

title: Environmental Goods Agreement

definition.text: Talks among 18 World Trade Organization members, begun in 2015, to cut tariffs on goods used to protect the environment.

facts.text: In trade usage, 'environmental goods' means products used to protect the environment, such as renewable energy technology and pollution control systems.
The talks aimed to spread cleaner technologies for air pollution control, waste treatment, renewable energy, monitoring and energy efficiency.
The negotiations collapsed in 2016.

notes: Uses a different sense of 'environmental good' (traded green technologies); may belong in a trade chapter.

title: Georgism

definition.text: The economic idea that people should own what they produce, but the income that comes from land and natural resources should belong equally to everyone in society.

facts.text: It grew from the writings of American economist Henry George, whose first book, Progress and Poverty (1879), argued for raising public money mainly from land and natural resources.
Its main policy is a land value tax, whose revenue could cut or replace taxes on income, trade and purchases.
In economics, 'land' means everything in nature that exists without human effort; George included climate, soil, waterways, minerals, forests, oceans, air and solar energy.
Milton Friedman called a tax on unimproved land value the 'least bad tax', because it does not hold back economic activity the way other taxes do.
Some Georgists want surplus revenue returned to people as a basic income or citizen's dividend.
George blamed private capture of land rent for persistent poverty despite technological progress, and for boom-and-bust cycles.

notes: Needs 'Economic rent' as a prerequisite if that entry exists elsewhere in the course.

definition.text: The Georgist view that pollution is a taking from the commons, so its value should be captured for the public through taxes or quotas.

facts.text: Henry George partly inspired the early conservation movement of the Progressive Era.
Some ecological economists back a land value tax as a way to free up unused land for rewilding and to curb urban sprawl.
Georgists and ecological economists both favor market-based limits on pollution, but Georgists stress that the resulting income should not go to polluters.
'Cap and share', the Georgist version of cap and trade, would auction temporary pollution permits and give the proceeds to the public instead of handing permits free to polluters.

definition.text: A public good available more or less worldwide, which no one can be kept from and whose use by one does not reduce it for others.

facts.text: The idea extends Paul Samuelson's notion of public goods to the global economy.
Knowledge is the classic example, including freely released projects such as free software and Wikipedia.
Kaul and colleagues (2003) note that some goods are public only by default, such as the ozone layer before anyone understood the damage from CFCs.
Climate change mitigation, financial stability, security, knowledge and global public health need international or supranational bodies to manage them, since national laws stop at borders.
A firm that saves money by polluting shared air or water becomes a corporate free rider, raising the cost of these often transnational public goods.
Because water crosses political borders, it cannot be managed by local or national authorities alone, and leaving it to the market would hurt those most in need.

title: Land tenure

definition.text: The system that decides who may use land, for how long and on what conditions.

facts.text: Tenure can rest on official laws and policies or on informal local customs.
It sets out the holder's rights and responsibilities toward the land.
Forms include fee simple, the most complete ownership in common law, as well as leasehold, life estates, common land rights, sharecropping and easements.
Land tenure and forest governance were named among the issues national REDD+ forest strategies must address.
Tradeable individual ownership of land was often introduced through colonialism.

notes: Long 'By country' section on foreign ownership bans skipped as country-specific.

definition.text: Indigenous ways of holding land, which in North America rested on stewardship rather than the control at the heart of European ownership.

facts.text: European settlers in North America sometimes ignored traditional tenure and seized land, and sometimes recognized it as aboriginal title.
Traditional communities in Brazil, such as fundos de pasto and faxinais, still practice communal land use.

definition.text: A tax, proposed by Swedish economist Erik Lindahl, in which each person pays for a public good according to the extra benefit they get from one more unit of it.

facts.text: Lindahl put forward the idea in 1919, influenced by his teacher Knut Wicksell, to show that agreement on public spending is possible.
If each person's tax price equals their own marginal benefit at the ideal level, everyone is better off and may agree to that level of provision.
In a worked example, a park costs $15 per acre; Sarah and Tom together will pay $15 at the 60th acre, so Sarah pays $5 and Tom $10 for each of 60 acres.
In theory it provides public goods efficiently, but it needs each person's demand, which is hard to know in practice.
People may understate their benefits to pay less, may not know their own valuation (for national defense, say), and government may struggle to add valuations up.

definition.text: The problem of finding out how much the public really wants a public good, when there is no market to make people show what it is worth to them.

facts.text: Without full knowledge of people's preferences, government planners are likely to supply too much or too little of a public good.
Since only individuals know their own benefit, they have a reason to understate it, a form of free riding.
Mechanisms such as Vickrey-Clarke-Groves aim to draw out true values, but none has fully solved the problem, and asking a large population is costly in money and time.

definition.text: A school of economics that studies the institutions, meaning the legal rules and social norms, that underlie economic activity.

facts.text: It assumes people are rational but have limited minds and information and find agreements hard to enforce, so institutions arise largely to cut transaction costs.
It grew from Ronald Coase's papers 'The Nature of the Firm' (1937) and 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960); Oliver Williamson coined the name in 1975.
Following Douglass North, institutions are 'the rules of the game', formal laws and informal norms, while organizations are the teams that play.
Associated Nobel laureates include Daron Acemoglu, Ronald Coase, Douglass North, Elinor Ostrom and Oliver Williamson.
Critics say it overlooks the coercion and power politics involved in creating and keeping institutions.

conflicts.text: In 1972 Harold Demsetz and Armen Alchian published the work described as founding New Institutional Economics.
conflicts.note: The NIE page dates the name to Williamson in 1975; this is a founding claim rather than the coining, so not strictly the same quantity.

definition.text: A useful good that its owner can keep others from using and that one person's use uses up for others.

facts.text: Bread is a private good: a loaf one person eats cannot be eaten by another, and a baker can refuse to sell it.
Private goods are scarce, which can create competition for them.
Unlike public goods such as clean air, private goods rarely suffer from free riding.
Market demand for a private good is found by adding up how much each person will buy at each price (horizontal summation), unlike public goods, whose individual demands are summed vertically.

title: Private property

definition.text: Ownership of property by people or organizations other than the government.

facts.text: It differs from public property, owned by the state, and from collective or cooperative property.
Private property is a legal idea defined and enforced by each country's legal and political institutions, and it is the foundation of capitalism.
John Locke's chief argument for owning land privately was that it led to better land management and farming than common land.
Supporters say private ownership puts land to productive use, protects its value, and lets it be traded or used as collateral.
Owners' rights usually come with limits, such as building codes or bans on demolishing historic buildings.
Socialists criticize private ownership of the means of production, and critics also call property law a tool of empire that ignored Indigenous common ownership of land.

contested_note: Economic liberals see private property as essential to prosperity, while socialists and other critics see it as a source of exploitation, inequality and land appropriation.

title: Property

definition.text: A system of rights that gives people legal control over valuable things, and also the valuable things themselves.

facts.text: Depending on the thing, an owner may use, change, share, rent, sell, give away or destroy it, and keep others from doing so.
Economics recognizes four broad forms: private, public, collective and common property.
Legal systems usually separate land and buildings (real property) from movable things (personal property), and tangible from intangible property.
One view holds that things become property only when they are scarce: hunter-gatherers did not treat land as property because there was no shortage of it.
Aristotle favored private property, arguing that self-interest leads people to neglect the commons.

notes: Overlaps heavily with 'Property rights'; may be folded into it.

definition.text: The mirror image of a public good: something harmful that no one can avoid and that harms everyone at once, such as air pollution.

facts.text: While markets supply too little of a public good, they supply too much of a public bad, because those causing it ignore the harm to others.
One way to reduce a public bad is for a third party, usually the state, to step in.
Deforestation, excess water use and pesticide use can be seen as public bads that push harm onto present and future generations.
Much of environmental economics is about externalities or 'public bads'.
Green economists suggest judging such impacts as far ahead as the seventh generation.

definition.text: The study of government policy in terms of efficiency and fairness, asking whether and how far government should take part in markets.

facts.text: It builds on welfare economics and aims to improve social welfare.
It focuses on market failures such as public goods, externalities and imperfect competition, and on taxes and government spending.
Government examples include providing defense, regulating pollution and dealing with unequal information between buyers and sellers.
A.C. Pigou proposed taxes to correct externalities, such as an emissions tax; in 1960 Ronald Coase proposed instead assigning property rights and letting people negotiate.
Much of cost-benefit analysis was developed in the United States from the problems of water-resource projects.

definition.text: The 1971 result by Peter Diamond and James Mirrlees that production efficiency is still desirable even when a government cannot use lump-sum taxes.

facts.text: It is credited with modernizing Ramsey's analysis of taxation by considering income distribution together with raising revenue.
Joseph Stiglitz and Partha Dasgupta (1971) argued it is not robust if some tax tools cannot be used.

title: Public trust doctrine

definition.text: The principle that the state holds certain resources, such as the shore between high and low tide, in trust for public use, whoever owns the land beside them.

facts.text: It goes back to Roman law, which held air, flowing water, the sea and the seashore to be common to all and not open to ownership.
It passed into English law and later into the common law of the United States, where it covers tidal and navigable waters and the minerals and animals in them.
It has been used to claim public interest in oil under tidal lands and to stop private ownership of fish stocks and shellfish beds.
Some countries have used it to protect natural resources as a human right, and protections are spreading to a global scale.

notes: Much of the page is US state law; kept for its general principle and Roman origins.

definition.text: A Roman law idea of things common to all humankind, such as air, running water, the sea and its shores, that came before modern ideas of the commons.

facts.text: The Institutes of Justinian codified it in the 6th century.
It differs from res publica, public property managed by government, since common things are for everyone to use and enjoy.
In environmental law it means the state is trustee of shared natural resources and cannot sell them into private hands.
Fish and mammals on the high seas are examples, and the rules for Antarctica and for space law were built on it.

definition.text: Paul Samuelson's rule for the best amount of a public good: provide more as long as the total of everyone's extra benefit is at least the extra cost of providing it.

facts.text: Formally, the sum of all consumers' marginal rates of substitution equals the economy's marginal rate of transformation between the public good and a private good.
For a private good, by contrast, each consumer's own valuation is set equal to the cost of producing one more unit.
Because everyone enjoys a public good at once, individual demands are added together vertically, so the rule extends supply and demand from private to public goods.
If two people would pay $200 and $100 for a park costing $225, its $300 total value leaves a $75 surplus, so it should be built.
Samuelson stressed that people have reasons to understate their valuations, which makes applying the rule hard in practice.

definition.text: A situation where people act for short-term personal gain in a way that, in the long run, leaves the whole group worse off.

facts.text: John Platt introduced the term in a 1973 paper, applying behavioral psychology to Hardin's tragedy of the commons.
Social traps are blamed for overfishing, overgrazing in the Sahel, rainforest destruction and, above all, climate change.
Choosing a car over public transport is a social trap: comfort now, more greenhouse gas emissions later.
Platt proposed rewards for green behavior and penalties such as pollution taxes as ways out.

definition.text: A situation where each person does better by acting selfishly whatever others do, yet everyone would do best if all cooperated.

facts.text: Robyn Dawes coined the term a few years after Platt, to cover both social traps and commons dilemmas.
There are three main kinds: large-scale dilemmas, commons (resource) dilemmas and public goods dilemmas.
Uncertainty about others' actions or about the resource discourages cooperation, but a trustworthy leader who manages the resource fairly can restore it.

title: Tragedy of the anticommons

definition.text: The mirror image of the tragedy of the commons: when a resource has many owners who can each block its use, it ends up underused.

facts.text: Michael Heller introduced the term in a 1998 article, after seeing empty shops in post-communist Eastern European cities where too many parties held rights over each space.
Early aviation patents held by the Wright brothers and Glenn Curtiss blocked each other until the government created a patent pool in World War I.
Housing shortages in many western cities have been described this way, since zoning lets many stakeholders block new homes.
Remedies include eminent domain and patent pools or other licensing bodies.

contested_note: Heller and Eisenberg argue biological patents create an anticommons, while others, citing surveys of scientists, say they have not.

title: Usufruct

definition.text: The right to use someone else's property, often land, and to take its fruits or profits, without owning it or being allowed to damage it.

facts.text: It combines usus, the right to use a thing, and fructus, the right to profit from it, such as by selling crops; full ownership adds abusus, the right to sell or destroy it.
In some customary law systems of Indigenous peoples of the Americas, all land was publicly owned and people gained rights to use areas, without damaging the land's future productivity.
Thomas Jefferson wrote in 1789 that 'Earth belongs in usufruct to the living', meaning each generation may use the earth but must not impoverish it for those to come.
Western US water rights are usufruct rights that can be forfeited if the holder does not put their full allocation to beneficial use.

notes: Country-variation sections (France, Louisiana, Cuba, India) skipped.

title: Impure public good

definition.text: A good that is non-rival and non-excludable only partly or only some of the time.

facts.text: Some parts of cybersecurity, such as sharing threat information and protecting critical infrastructure and election integrity, behave like impure public goods.
Public property is sometimes treated as a public good, usually an impure one.
Since pure public goods are rare, most goods called public are impure in practice.

notes: Phrase concept with no page. S:08a4186c998e also equates open-access property with 'impure public good', a usage inconsistent with the Public good page; not used.
